column9: Match each inheritance pattern to its description.
column14: Incomplete dominance :: The heterozygote is an in-between blend
column15: Codominance :: Both alleles show fully in the heterozygote
column16: Multiple alleles :: More than two alleles of one gene exist in the population
column17: Sex-linked trait :: The gene is on the X chromosome but not the Y
column18: Polygenic trait :: Many genes add together to control one trait
column28: Incomplete dominance gives an in-between blend in the heterozygote, while codominance shows both alleles fully at the same time. Multiple alleles means a gene has more than two alleles in the population. A sex-linked trait's gene is on the X chromosome but not the Y. A polygenic trait is controlled by many genes adding together.
column29: For each term, ask: is it about what the heterozygote looks like, how many alleles a gene has, how many genes there are, or which chromosome the gene is on?

column9: In horses, a chestnut (reddish-brown) parent and a cream-white parent can have a palomino foal, with a golden coat color in between the two parents' colors. Which inheritance pattern is this?
column15: Sex-linked inheritance
column17: Multiple alleles
column28: Golden palomino is an in-between blend of chestnut and cream-white, so this is incomplete dominance. In codominance, both parent colors would show at the same time, side by side, instead of one in-between color. Sex-linked traits are on the X chromosome, and multiple alleles means more than two alleles for a gene.
column29: Is the foal's color a blend of the parents, or do both parent colors show up separately?

column9: Roan cattle have a coat with red hairs **and** white hairs mixed together. Their parents were a red bull and a white cow. Which inheritance pattern is this?
column15: Polygenic inheritance
column17: Sex-linked inheritance
column28: Each hair is fully red or fully white: both alleles show up completely, which is codominance. Incomplete dominance would give a blend (pink hairs). Polygenic traits show a smooth range from many genes, and sex-linked traits are carried on the X chromosome.
column29: Are the hairs a blended color, or do both colors show fully?

column9: The ABO blood type gene has three alleles: A, B, and O. Counting AO and OA as the same genotype, there are ___ different ABO genotypes.
column20: 6|six|6 genotypes|six genotypes|6 different genotypes|six different genotypes|6 ABO genotypes|six ABO genotypes
column28: There are six: AA, AO, BB, BO, AB, and OO. Each one is a different pair of the three alleles, including the pairs with two of the same allele (AA, BB, and OO). Nine counts mixed pairs like AO and OA twice, and four is the number of blood types, not the number of genotypes.
column29: Make an organized list so you don't miss any or count any twice, and don't forget pairs with two of the same allele, like AA.

column9: A person has the blood type genotype **AO**. What is the person's blood type?
column15: Type AB
column17: Type A
column28: A is dominant over O, so AO gives type A blood (just like AA). Type O needs OO, type AB needs both A and B, and type B would need a B allele, which AO doesn't have.
column29: Which allele is recessive in the ABO system?

column9: Which genotypes give a person type **B** blood?
column15: BB or BO
column17: BB, BO, or AB
column28: B is dominant over O, so both BB and BO give type B blood. AB gives type AB, because A and B are codominant (both show).
column29: B is dominant over one allele and codominant with the other.

column9: Put the steps for solving a sex-linked (X-linked) Punnett square in order.
column14: Fill in each box with one allele from the mother and one from the father.
column15: Write each parent's genotype with the sex chromosomes, like X^{H}X^{h} or X^{H}Y.
column16: Answer the question for sons, daughters, or all children, as the problem asks.
column17: Put the mother's two X alleles on one side and the father's X and Y on the other side.
column18: Sort the boxes into daughters (XX) and sons (XY).
column28: Start with genotypes that include the X and Y chromosomes, set up the square with the mother's X's on one side and the father's X and Y on the other, fill in the boxes, sort them into daughters (XX) and sons (XY), and then answer what the question asks: sons only, daughters only, or all children.
column29: You can't sort the boxes into sons and daughters until the boxes are filled in.

column9: Males are more likely than females to show an X-linked recessive trait because males have only one X chromosome.
column28: True. A male (XY) has only one X, so one recessive allele is enough to show the trait; the Y has no matching allele to cover it up. A female needs the recessive allele on both X chromosomes.
column29: How many copies of an X-linked gene does a male have?

column9: For hemophilia, **H** is normal blood clotting and **h** is hemophilia. A woman has the genotype X^{H}X^{h}. Which describes her?
column15: She cannot pass hemophilia on to her children
column16: She is a carrier with normal blood clotting
column17: She is homozygous for normal clotting
column28: X^{H}X^{h} has one normal allele that covers the recessive h, so her blood clots normally, but she carries h and can pass it to her children. She would have hemophilia only as X^{h}X^{h}, and she is heterozygous, not homozygous.
column29: One allele is dominant and one is recessive. Which one shows, and which one is hidden but can still be passed on?

column9: From which parent does a son get his **X** chromosome?
column15: His father
column17: Both of his parents
column28: A son is XY. His Y must come from his father (mothers have no Y), so his X comes from his mother. That's why sons get X-linked traits from their mothers.
column29: Which parent is the only one who can give a Y chromosome?

column9: In a made-up breed of mouse, coat color shows **incomplete dominance**. **YY** mice are yellow, and **WW** mice are white. What color fur would a **YW** mouse most likely have?
column14: Yellow fur, because Y is dominant over W
column15: Cream fur, a blend of yellow and white
column16: White fur, because W is dominant over Y
column17: Patches of yellow fur and white fur side by side
column28: In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote is an in-between blend of the two homozygous forms, so a YW mouse has cream fur, a blend of yellow and white. All yellow or all white would mean one allele is completely dominant, and separate yellow and white patches would be codominance.
column29: Think of snapdragons: how does a pink RW flower compare with a red RR flower and a white WW flower?

column9: In **codominance**, the heterozygous offspring shows a blend of the parents' traits, like a pink flower from red and white parents.
column28: False. That describes incomplete dominance. In codominance, both alleles show fully at the same time, like red and white patches, or type AB blood with both A and B.
column29: Blend is one pattern; both showing fully is the other.

column9: Human height comes in a smooth range of values instead of just a few separate categories like "tall" and "short." Which explains this best?
column14: Height is a sex-linked trait carried on the X chromosome
column15: Height is controlled by one gene with two alleles
column16: Height is a codominant trait controlled by one gene
column17: Height is a polygenic trait controlled by many genes
column28: Height is polygenic: many genes each add a little, and the environment (like nutrition) also matters, so people show a smooth range. One gene gives just a few categories, whether its alleles are dominant and recessive or codominant, and sex-linked inheritance isn't what makes a smooth range.
column29: A smooth range comes from many small effects adding together.

column9: Which blood type is called the **universal donor**, because it can be given to people of every ABO blood type?
column15: Type B
column17: Type O
column28: Type O blood has no A or B antigens, so no one's anti-A or anti-B antibodies attack it. Type AB is the universal receiver. Types A and B each carry an antigen that some people's antibodies would attack.
column29: Which blood type has no A or B antigens on its red blood cells?

column9: Can a male be a carrier (have the allele but not show it) for an X-linked recessive trait?
column14: Yes, if he is heterozygous for the trait
column15: No, because males cannot inherit X-linked alleles
column16: Yes, if his Y chromosome has a dominant allele to cover it
column17: No, because the allele on his only X always shows
column28: A male has only one X. If it carries the recessive allele, there is no second X to hide it, so he shows the trait. The Y chromosome doesn't carry these genes, so it can't cover the allele. Being heterozygous takes two copies of the gene, which a male doesn't have. Males do inherit X-linked alleles, from their mothers.
column29: To be a carrier, you need a second allele to cover up the recessive one. Does a male have a second X?

column9: In a species of tropical fish, scale color shows incomplete dominance. **BB** fish are blue, **YY** fish are yellow, and **BY** fish are green. Addy crosses two green fish (**BY × BY**). What percent of the babies are expected to be green? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: BY × BY → BB, BY, BY, YY. Two of the 4 boxes are BY (green) = 50%. The other babies are 25% blue (BB) and 25% yellow (YY).
column29: Green is the heterozygous blend. How many of the 4 boxes have one B and one Y?

column9: In four o'clock flowers, **RR** is red, **WW** is white, and **RW** is pink. Jae crosses a pink plant with a white plant (**RW × WW**). What phenotype ratio should Jae expect?
column15: 3 pink : 1 white
column17: All pink
column28: Punnett square: RW × WW → RW, RW, WW, WW: 2 pink : 2 white, or 1 pink : 1 white. No red is possible because the white parent has no R, so any ratio with red in it (like 1:2:1) is wrong. 3:1 is a simple-dominance ratio, and all pink would need RW in every box, which this cross can't give.
column29: The white parent can only give W. What can the pink parent give?

column9: In snapdragons, **RR** flowers are red, **WW** flowers are white, and **RW** flowers are pink. Two pink snapdragons are crossed (**RW × RW**). The expected phenotype ratio red : pink : white is ___.
column28: Punnett square: RW × RW → RR, RW, RW, WW: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. In incomplete dominance the genotype ratio and the phenotype ratio match, because the heterozygote has its own look. There is no 3:1 here.
column29: Fill in the square, and remember that RW is its own color.

column9: In cattle, the alleles C^{R} (red hair) and C^{W} (white hair) are codominant. Cattle that are C^{R}C^{W} are roan, with red hairs and white hairs. Two roan cattle are crossed. What percent of their calves are expected to be **red**? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: C^{R}C^{W} × C^{R}C^{W} → C^{R}C^{R} (red), C^{R}C^{W} (roan), C^{R}C^{W} (roan), C^{W}C^{W} (white). Only 1 of the 4 boxes is red = 25%. Roan is 50% and white is 25%.
column29: Red calves need two C^{R} alleles. How many of the 4 boxes have that?

column9: In a breed of chickens, black (**BB**) and white (**WW**) feathers are codominant, so **BW** chickens are speckled with both black feathers and white feathers. A speckled hen is crossed with a white rooster. What should their chicks look like?
column15: All gray, a blend of black and white
column17: 3 speckled : 1 white
column28: Punnett square: BW × WW → BW, BW, WW, WW: half speckled and half white (1:1). The white rooster can only give W, so no chick can be black (BB), which rules out any ratio with black chicks in it. Gray would be a blend, which is incomplete dominance, not codominance, and only 2 of the 4 boxes are speckled, not 3.
column29: The white rooster can only give W. What can the speckled hen give?

column9: A woman with the genotype **AA** has children with a man whose genotype is **BO**. What blood types can their children have?
column15: Type A and type B
column17: Types A, B, AB, and O
column28: Punnett square: AA × BO → AB, AO, AB, AO. AB is type AB and AO is type A. No child can be type B or type O, because every child gets an A from the mother.
column29: The mother can only give A. What two alleles can the father give?

column9: Jacob's mother and father both have the genotype **BO**. What is the chance that a child of theirs has type **O** blood? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: BO × BO → BB, BO, BO, OO. Only OO is type O: 1 of 4 boxes = 25%. Two type B parents can have a type O child when both of them carry O.
column29: Type O needs two O alleles. Can both parents give an O?

column9: A woman with the genotype **BO** has children with a man who has type **AB** blood. What percent of their children are expected to have type **B** blood? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: A type AB man must be AB. Punnett square: BO × AB → AB (type AB), BB (type B), AO (type A), BO (type B). Type B = BB + BO = 2 of 4 boxes = 50%.
column29: Write the man's genotype first (type AB has only one possible genotype), then count the boxes that are BB or BO.

column9: A baby has type **O** blood, and the mother has type **A** blood. Which man could **not** be the baby's father?
column14: A man with type A blood
column15: A man with type B blood
column16: A man with type O blood
column17: A man with type AB blood
column28: A type O baby is OO, so the father must have an O allele to give. Type A (AO), type B (BO), and type O (OO) men can all carry O. A type AB man has no O allele, so he cannot be the father. (The mother must be AO.)
column29: The baby is OO. Which man has no O allele at all?

column9: In fruit flies, red eyes (X^{R}) are dominant over white eyes (X^{r}). A heterozygous red-eyed female (X^{R}X^{r}) is crossed with a red-eyed male (X^{R}Y). What fraction of the **male** offspring are expected to have white eyes?
column17: All of them
column28: Punnett square: X^{R}X^{r} × X^{R}Y → daughters X^{R}X^{R} and X^{R}X^{r} (all red-eyed); sons X^{R}Y (red) and X^{r}Y (white). Half of the males (1/2) have white eyes. 1/4 is the fraction of all offspring with white eyes, not the fraction of males.
column29: Sons get their only X from their mother. What two X's can she give?

column9: A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia (X^{H}X^{h}) has children with a man who has normal blood clotting (X^{H}Y). What percent of **all** their children are expected to have hemophilia? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: X^{H}X^{h} × X^{H}Y → X^{H}X^{H}, X^{H}X^{h}, X^{H}Y, X^{h}Y. Only X^{h}Y has hemophilia: 1 of 4 boxes = 25% of all children. The carrier daughter (X^{H}X^{h}) has normal clotting, so she isn't counted.
column29: Fill in all four boxes, then count only the boxes that would actually have hemophilia.

column9: A man with hemophilia (X^{h}Y) has children with a woman who is not a carrier (X^{H}X^{H}). Which describes their children?
column14: Half of the sons have hemophilia, and no daughters are carriers
column15: All daughters are carriers, and all sons have normal clotting
column16: All sons have hemophilia, and all daughters are carriers
column17: All sons are carriers, and all daughters have normal clotting
column28: Punnett square: X^{H}X^{H} × X^{h}Y → daughters X^{H}X^{h} (carriers with normal clotting) and sons X^{H}Y (normal). The father gives his X^{h} to every daughter and his Y to every son, so no son can get hemophilia from him, and every daughter is a carrier. Choices that give sons hemophilia mix up which children get the father's X, and males can't be carriers.
column29: Which children get the father's X, and which get his Y?

column9: For red-green colorblindness, **B** is normal vision and **b** is colorblind. Which genotypes belong to a person with **normal** color vision? Select all that apply.
column15: X^{B}X^{b}
column17: X^{B}Y
column28: Anyone with at least one X^{B} has normal vision: X^{B}X^{B} (normal female), X^{B}X^{b} (carrier female with normal vision), and X^{B}Y (normal male). X^{b}X^{b} and X^{b}Y are colorblind because there is no X^{B} to cover the b.
column29: B is dominant and b is recessive. For each genotype, decide which allele shows, and remember how many X chromosomes a male has.

column9: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is X-linked recessive (**D** = normal muscles, **d** = DMD). Two parents with normal muscles have a son with DMD. What are the parents' genotypes?
column15: Mother X^{D}X^{D}, father X^{d}Y
column17: Mother X^{d}X^{d}, father X^{D}Y
column28: The son is X^{d}Y, and his X came from his mother, so she must carry d. She has normal muscles, so she is a carrier, X^{D}X^{d}. The father has normal muscles, so he is X^{D}Y. X^{d}Y would mean the father has DMD, and X^{d}X^{d} would mean the mother has DMD.
column29: Where did the son's only X come from?

column9: In radishes, root shape shows incomplete dominance: **LL** roots are long, **RR** roots are round, and **LR** roots are oval. Storm crosses an oval radish with a round radish (**LR × RR**). What percent of the offspring are expected to be **oval**? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: LR × RR → LR, LR, RR, RR. Two of the 4 boxes are LR (oval) = 50%. The other 50% are round, and no long radishes are possible because the round parent has no L to give.
column29: Put L and R from the oval parent on one side and R and R from the round parent on the other. How many boxes have one L and one R?

column9: In camellias, **RR** plants have red flowers, **WW** plants have white flowers, and **RW** plants have red-and-white patched flowers. Ana crosses two camellias and gets 40 offspring: 10 red, 20 patched, and 10 white. What were the parents' phenotypes?
column14: One parent was red and the other was white
column15: One parent was patched and the other was white
column16: Both parents had red-and-white patched flowers
column17: One parent was red and the other was patched
column28: Red, patched, and white offspring all appear, so each parent had to be able to give both R and W. Only a patched (RW) parent can do that, so both parents were patched. If either parent were red (RR), no white offspring could appear, and if either parent were white (WW), no red offspring could appear.
column29: Red offspring need an R from each parent, and white offspring need a W from each parent. Which parents can give both?

column9: Two purebred lines of a plant are crossed: one has purple flowers and one has white flowers. Which result in the offspring would show that flower color is **codominant**, not incompletely dominant?
column14: Every offspring has light purple (lavender) flowers
column15: Every offspring has flowers with separate purple and white streaks
column17: Half of the offspring are purple and half are white
column28: Codominance means both alleles show fully, so purple and white appear side by side as streaks. Lavender would be a blend (incomplete dominance), all purple would mean purple is completely dominant, and two purebred parents can't give a 1:1 split.
column29: Codominance: both colors show completely, at the same time.

column9: Height is a polygenic trait. Two parents who are both of medium height can have a child who grows up to be taller than either parent.
column28: True. Height is controlled by many genes, and each parent carries a mix of "taller" and "shorter" alleles for those genes. Each child gets a random half of each parent's alleles, so by chance a child can inherit more "taller" alleles than either parent has and end up taller than both.
column29: Think about many genes, each with "taller" and "shorter" alleles. Does a child have to get the same mix that a parent has?

column9: People with type **A** blood have anti-B antibodies in their plasma. From which blood types can a person with type A blood **receive** blood safely?
column15: A, B, AB, and O
column17: A and O
column28: A type A person's anti-B antibodies would attack any blood with B antigens (types B and AB). Type A blood (A antigens only) and type O blood (no A or B antigens) are safe. "A and AB" is the list of types that type A can give to. Only type AB can receive from all four.
column29: Cross out any donor blood that has B antigens on it.

column9: There are three ABO alleles (A, B, and O) in the human population. How many ABO alleles does each person have?
column15: Two
column17: It depends on the blood type
column28: Multiple alleles means more than two alleles exist in the population, but each person still has just two, one from each parent. That's why blood type genotypes are written with two letters, like AO or AB.
column29: Think about the difference between how many alleles exist in the whole population and how many one person inherits. Where does each of your alleles come from?

column9: A hospital record says that a baby with type **AB** blood was born to a mother with type **O** blood. What is the best conclusion?
column14: The father must have type AB blood
column15: The father must have type A or type B blood
column16: The record must contain a mistake
column17: This is possible if the father has type O blood
column28: A type O mother is OO, so she can only pass on O. A type AB baby needs an A and a B, one from each parent, so the mother would have to give A or B. That's impossible, so the record must be wrong, no matter who the father is.
column29: The baby needs two alleles, one from each parent. What allele can a type O mother give?

column9: Maya has type A blood, but her father has type O blood. Her husband has type B blood, but his mother has type O blood. What is the chance that their child will have type **AB** blood? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Maya got an O from her type O (OO) father, so she is AO. Her husband got an O from his OO mother, so he is BO. Punnett square: AO × BO → AB, AO, BO, OO. Type AB = 1 of 4 boxes = 25%.
column29: First figure out each parent's genotype. What allele did each of them have to get from their type O parent?

column9: Wyatt has type **O** blood, and his sister has type **AB** blood. What must their parents' genotypes be?
column15: AO and BO
column17: AO and AB
column28: Wyatt is OO, so each parent has an O. His sister is AB, so one parent gave A and the other gave B. The only parents with both are AO and BO. AA × BB can't make an O child, AB × OO can't make an O or an AB child, and AO × AB can't make an O child (the AB parent has no O).
column29: Each child got one allele from each parent. Which alleles must each parent carry to make both an OO child and an AB child?

column9: A woman with normal blood clotting, whose father had hemophilia, has children with a man who has normal clotting. What percent of their **sons** are expected to have hemophilia? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Her father (X^{h}Y) gave her his X^{h}, so she is a carrier, X^{H}X^{h}. Punnett square: X^{H}X^{h} × X^{H}Y → sons X^{H}Y and X^{h}Y. Half of the sons (50%) are expected to have hemophilia.
column29: Daughters always get their father's X. What does that tell you about the woman's genotype?

column9: A colorblind man (X^{b}Y) has children with a woman who is homozygous for normal vision (X^{B}X^{B}). One of their daughters later has children with a man who has normal vision. What percent of **all** the daughter's children, sons and daughters together, are expected to be colorblind? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: First cross: X^{B}X^{B} × X^{b}Y → every daughter is X^{B}X^{b} (a carrier). Second cross: X^{B}X^{b} × X^{B}Y → X^{B}X^{B}, X^{B}X^{b}, X^{B}Y, X^{b}Y. Only X^{b}Y is colorblind: 1 of the 4 boxes = 25% of all her children. Counting only the sons' boxes answers a different question, and none of her daughters are colorblind. The trait skipped a generation through a carrier daughter.
column29: Do two crosses. What must the daughter's genotype be after the first cross?

column9: In cats, a fur color gene is on the X chromosome. X^{B} gives black fur and X^{b} gives yellow fur. A female with both alleles (X^{B}X^{b}) is tortoiseshell, with black and yellow patches. A tortoiseshell female is crossed with a black male (X^{B}Y). What percent of the kittens are expected to be **black**? Answer in %, as a number like 80.
column28: Punnett square: X^{B}X^{b} × X^{B}Y → X^{B}X^{B} (black female), X^{B}X^{b} (tortoiseshell female), X^{B}Y (black male), X^{b}Y (yellow male). Black = 2 of 4 boxes = 50%. Tortoiseshell is 25% (daughters only) and yellow is 25% (sons only).
column29: Fill in all four boxes, then count both the black daughters and the black sons.

column9: A colorblind woman (X^{b}X^{b}) has children with a man who has normal vision (X^{B}Y). Which statement is true about their children?
column14: All sons are colorblind, and all daughters are carriers with normal vision
column15: Half of the sons and half of the daughters are colorblind
column16: All of the children are colorblind
column17: None of the children are colorblind, because the father has normal vision
column28: Punnett square: X^{b}X^{b} × X^{B}Y → daughters X^{B}X^{b} (normal vision, carriers) and sons X^{b}Y (colorblind). Every son gets X^{b} from his mother and a Y from his father, so all sons are colorblind. Every daughter gets her father's X^{B}, so none of the daughters are colorblind.
column29: The mother can only give X^{b}. What does each son get from his father, and what does each daughter get?

column9: Which statements about X-linked recessive traits are true? Select all that apply.
column14: A father passes his X-linked allele to all of his daughters.
column15: A father passes his X-linked allele to all of his sons.
column16: A carrier mother can pass the allele to both sons and daughters.
column17: A daughter who shows the trait must have a father who shows the trait.
column18: A male can be a carrier who does not show the trait.
column28: Fathers give their X to every daughter and their Y to every son, so a father's X-linked allele goes to all of his daughters and none of his sons. A carrier mother can pass X^{h} to any child. An affected daughter is X^{h}X^{h}, so she got an X^{h} from her father, who must be X^{h}Y and affected. Males have only one X, so they can't be carriers.
column29: Test each statement with a quick Punnett square using real genotypes, like X^{h}Y and X^{H}X^{h}. Select a statement only if it is true every time.

column9: Saffron is growing four o'clock flowers, where **RR** is red, **WW** is white, and **RW** is pink. She wants the **most** pink flowers possible. Which cross should she make?
column15: Red × white
column17: Red × pink
column28: Red × white (RR × WW) puts RW in all 4 boxes: 100% pink. Pink × pink gives only 50% pink (1 red : 2 pink : 1 white), and pink × white or red × pink each give 50% pink.
column29: Make a Punnett square for each choice. Which one puts RW in every box?

column9: In cattle, C^{R} (red) and C^{W} (white) are codominant, and C^{R}C^{W} cattle are roan. A farmer near Cadott crosses a roan bull with red cows (C^{R}C^{R}) and gets 30 calves. About how many of the calves are expected to be roan?
column28: Punnett square: C^{R}C^{W} × C^{R}C^{R} → C^{R}C^{R}, C^{R}C^{R}, C^{R}C^{W}, C^{R}C^{W}. Half are roan, so about 1/2 × 30 = 15 calves. The other 15 are red, and no white calves are possible.
column29: Find the fraction of boxes that are C^{R}C^{W}, then take that fraction of 30.

column9: Mila measures 100 ears of corn from one field and sorts them by length. Data table: ear length (cm): 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24 | number of ears: 3, 10, 22, 30, 22, 10, 3. Which inheritance pattern do these data best support?
column14: Polygenic, because there are many length groups in a bell shape
column15: Simple dominance, because the 18 cm group is the most common
column16: Incomplete dominance, because the middle groups are the biggest
column17: Codominance, because both short ears and long ears appear
column28: The data show many length groups that rise smoothly to a peak in the middle and fall off on both sides: a bell-shaped curve. That comes from many genes each adding a small amount to ear length. One gene with complete dominance gives only 2 phenotypes (3:1), and one gene with incomplete dominance or codominance gives only 3 phenotypes (1:2:1). The most common group isn't the "dominant" one, and a big middle group doesn't mean incomplete dominance when there are 7 groups, not 3.
column29: Count how many different length groups there are. How many phenotypes can one gene with two alleles make?

column9: Jae takes cuttings (pieces of stem that grow into new plants) from one plant, so all of the new plants have identical genes. Half grow in rich soil with lots of light, and half grow in poor soil in the shade. The first group grows much taller. What does this show?
column14: The plants in poor soil inherited different height alleles
column15: Soil and light changed the plants' height alleles

column9: In a species of beetle, a cross of green-shelled females with brown-shelled males gives all green offspring. The reverse cross, brown-shelled females with green-shelled males, gives green daughters and brown sons. What best explains why the results differ?
column15: The brown allele is dominant in males only
column16: Shell color is controlled by many genes
column17: The shell color gene is on the X chromosome
column28: When the results change depending on which parent shows the trait, and sons and daughters differ, the gene is on the X chromosome. With G = green and g = brown, brown mothers (X^{g}X^{g}) give X^{g} to every son, so all the sons are brown, while every daughter also gets X^{G} from her green father and is green. If brown were dominant in males only, the first cross's sons would get a brown allele from their brown father and be brown, but they are green. Incomplete dominance would give an in-between color, and a polygenic trait would not make sons and daughters differ like this.
column29: Compare the sons in the two crosses. Which parent's color do the sons match each time?
